kurz: An index is a calculation rule with three specifications: which securities are included, how much weight they carry and what counts as return.

bloecke.md:
An index is a calculation rule and neither a fund nor a portfolio. The rule consists of three decisions: which securities are included, how much weight each security carries and what counts as return. With these three pieces of information, you can classify an index within a few minutes. It also becomes clear why two curves that are both supposed to represent “the market” follow completely different paths.

Index providers are companies with their own business model. MSCI, FTSE Russell, S&P Dow Jones, Solactive and the index subsidiary of Deutsche Börse sell licences to fund management companies. The provider earns nothing from an index that no fund tracks. That is why there is a suitable index for almost every investment idea. For the same reason, it is more important to know which index a product tracks than what the product is called.

## Selection by rulebook or by committee

Inclusion in an index follows either fixed rules or the judgement of a committee. MSCI and FTSE Russell work on a rules basis. There, a security must reach a minimum size in terms of free float market capitalisation, show minimum liquidity and be listed in a country that the provider classifies as a developed or emerging market. In this way, the MSCI World covers around 85% of the free float market capitalisation in each country. The rest, mainly small companies, is not included.

The S&P 500, by contrast, is compiled by a committee. There are criteria such as being domiciled in the US, a minimum size, sufficient free float and profits in recent quarters. However, a company that meets them is not automatically included, because the committee decides on this. The S&P 500 therefore contains 500 selected US companies, which are not necessarily the 500 largest.

Since the 2021 reform, the DAX has been governed by purely rules-based criteria. The ranking depends solely on free float market capitalisation; order book turnover now only serves as evidence of minimum liquidity. In addition, there is a profitability hurdle and the requirement for audited financial statements. Both additions are a direct consequence of the Wirecard case. With a balance sheet that was false in material respects, Wirecard remained in the benchmark index until its insolvency.

bloecke.formel: Index weight = (Price × Number of shares × Free float factor) / Sum of all values calculated in this way
bloecke.erklaerung: The usual stock indices weight by market capitalisation but only take the freely tradable portion into account. Stakes held by founding families, governments or strategic major shareholders are excluded via the free float factor, because they cannot be bought on the market.
variablen: Proportion of freely tradable shares, usually rounded in bands
bloecke.beispiel: Two companies are each worth €100 billion. At A, 90% of the shares are freely tradable, at B only 40%, because a family holds the rest. A enters the index with €90 billion, B with €40 billion. Although both companies are the same size, A therefore has more than twice the index weight of B.

bloecke.md: The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the Nikkei 225 weight by share price instead of by market value. A share priced at €400 counts four times as much there as one priced at €100, regardless of how large the two companies are. This method dates from the time before the pocket calculator and has no economic justification. A share split changes nothing about the company but shifts the weights in these indices.

## Price index or total return index

The third decision, what counts as return, is the one most often overlooked. A **price return index** (price index) measures only price movements. A **total return index** assumes that every dividend is immediately reinvested in the index.

The DAX has been a total return index since its launch. It started at 1,000 points on 30 December 1987. A DAX price index is calculated in parallel, but hardly anyone quotes it. The S&P 500, the Nasdaq 100, the Euro Stoxx 50 and the Nikkei 225, by contrast, are usually quoted as price indices in public reporting. Total return versions do exist, but they do not appear in the news.

A performance comparison based on a DAX chart and an S&P 500 chart therefore sets a series with dividends against a series without dividends. Over decades, this difference distorts the comparison considerably, as the following illustrative calculation shows.

bloecke.md: First clarify whether both series use the same return convention. Comparing a price index with a total return index leads to a wrong result. ETF factsheets usually state “Net Total Return”. In this case, the dividends are reinvested, but after deducting the withholding tax that a foreign investor typically bears.

## Country weights of a world index

With capitalisation weighting, an index reflects how stock market value is distributed and not where economic output is generated. At the end of August 2026, the US accounted for around 72% of the MSCI World. This share follows logically from the rule, because US stock markets are so large by market value. A “world” product is therefore primarily an investment in American shares and in the dollar.

bloecke.titel: Country weights in the MSCI World, as of 31 Aug 2026
bloecke.unter: The index covers 23 developed markets, but around three quarters of the weight is in North America; emerging markets are not included.

## Number of index constituents

The number of securities included says little about the risk of an index but a lot about its construction. In its standard indices, MSCI leaves out small caps, whereas FTSE includes some of them. This explains the large gap in the number of constituents between the ACWI and the All-World, even though both cover almost the same countries. A second difference is purely a matter of definition. FTSE classifies South Korea as a developed market, MSCI as an emerging market. The same market is therefore classified differently depending on the rulebook.

bloecke.unter: The number of constituents grows by a factor of 100, but the share of the ten largest positions does not fall to the same extent.

punkte: Weights shift automatically with prices, without any need to trade
Very low turnover, and therefore low costs in the fund
All investors can hold it at the same time, because it reflects the market average
Leads automatically to concentration when a few securities dominate
Each security receives the same share, so 0.2% each in the S&P 500
Must be reset regularly by selling winners and buying losers
Higher turnover and higher transaction costs; the tax effect within the fund is of only limited relevance in Germany
Contains a systematic tilt towards smaller and more cheaply valued securities (sometimes an advantage, sometimes years of lagging behind)

bloecke.md: Equal-weighted versions are often marketed as “the better index” because they are frequently ahead in long backtests. This lead does not prove a superior construction. It results from the built-in tilt towards smaller companies and towards countercyclical rebalancing. In decades when returns come mainly from the largest securities, equal weighting lags well behind. Choosing an equal-weighted version is therefore an active decision and should be named as such.

## Index changes

Every index is reviewed regularly, usually quarterly; larger overhauls often take place once a year. In addition, there are special rules for takeovers, insolvencies or IPOs, under which a security is added or removed outside the regular cycle.

These adjustments give rise to the **index effect**. When an inclusion is announced, all index funds must buy the security by the effective date. This demand is forced and scheduled and can therefore be traded on, which active market participants have been exploiting for decades. As the passive market has grown and awareness of the effect has spread, it has become smaller, but it is still visible for small indices and large new additions.

The rulebook itself is also adjusted when the construction reaches its limits. The Nasdaq 100 has been reweighted outside the regular schedule several times, most recently in 2023, because a few technology shares had exceeded the internal concentration limit. An index is therefore a product whose rules the provider can change.

Secondary sources put the weight of the ten largest companies in the S&P 500 in 2026 at just under two fifths, compared with about a fifth in 2010. The exact figures differ depending on the data source, but the direction of the trend is undisputed. Investors who hold an S&P 500 ETF and an MSCI World ETF therefore buy the same companies twice and achieve no additional diversification, because US securities make up around 72% of the MSCI World.

## Requirements of fund law

An ETF may not replicate an index with any degree of concentration it likes. For ordinary UCITS (OGAW), the 5/10/40 rule of Section 206 KAGB (German Investment Code) applies: at most 5% per issuer, up to 10% if the investment conditions provide for it, and all positions above 5% together at most 40% of the fund assets.

Under Section 209 KAGB, index funds may by way of exception invest up to 20% per issuer, and up to 35% in a single issuer. This requires an index recognised by BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority) that is sufficiently diversified, represents the market adequately and is published in an appropriate manner. That is why many indices include a **weight cap** in their rulebook. It limits the weight of individual securities so that the index fits into a UCITS product at all. The cap is therefore a condition for constructing the product and not a protective rule out of concern for investors.

For broad indices, the fund often buys only a representative selection of the positions (optimised sampling). The iShares Core MSCI World holds around 1,250 securities, the Vanguard FTSE All-World around 3,780. Both thus replicate their indices almost completely, but the number in the factsheet may differ from the official number of index constituents. Such a deviation is not a warning sign, because with thousands of tiny positions, a selection is the more cost-effective solution. How well it has worked is shown by the tracking difference over several years and not by the number of securities.

1. Clarify whether it is a price index or a total return index and how the comparison series is calculated.
2. Check the number of securities and countries as well as the country classification.
3. Look at the largest single weight and the sum of the ten largest positions.
4. Clarify whether a rulebook or a committee decides on inclusions and how often the index is adjusted.

This information can be found in the provider's index methodology and in the ETF factsheet, not in the product name.

mitnehmen: An index is a calculation rule made up of three decisions: selection, weighting and return convention.
Because the DAX is a total return index and the S&P 500 is usually quoted as a price index, a direct chart comparison of the two is not meaningful.
Capitalisation weighting reflects how stock market value is distributed and not where economic output is generated; at the end of August 2026, around 72% of the MSCI World consisted of US securities.
The index weight depends on the free float, so two companies of the same size can differ in weight by more than a factor of two.
Section 209 KAGB allows index UCITS up to 20% per issuer and up to 35% in a single issuer; this is the main reason why indices have weight caps.

begriffe.text: The freely tradable portion of a company's shares. Fixed stakes held by families, governments or strategic investors are excluded; only the remaining portion determines the index weight.
Index that assumes all dividends are reinvested. The DAX is a total return index; a price index, by contrast, measures only the price movement.
Upper limit on the weight of an individual security, set out in the index rulebook. Among other things, it ensures that the index can still be replicated within the investment limits for UCITS funds.
Price movement that arises because index funds must buy a newly included security by the effective date and this demand is predictable.
Construction in which every index constituent receives the same share. It requires the weights to be reset regularly and contains a systematic tilt towards smaller companies.
